Direct answer: Yes — nothing stops a phylactery counter from going on Tatterkite, because Humility strips Tatterkite of the very ability that would forbid it. The bigger question is whether Phylactery Lich's counter-placing ability works at all.

Why Tatterkite can receive counters: Tatterkite's printed ability "This creature can't have counters put on it" is an ability that functions both as Tatterkite enters and while Tatterkite is on the battlefield [113.6i]. Humility says "All creatures lose all abilities and have base power and toughness 1/1," and ability-removing effects are applied in layer 6 [613.1f]. Once Humility is on the battlefield, Tatterkite has no abilities at all, so it has no "can't have counters put on it" restriction left to invoke; the "can't beats can" principle of [101.2a] expressly does not cover adding or removing abilities. Note this is a removal effect, not a "can't have that ability" effect of the [113.11] type, so it's simply gone. (Humility does not remove Tatterkite from the battlefield or change that it's a creature; it becomes a 1/1 with no abilities, and counters that modify power/toughness would still apply in layer 7c [613.4c].)

The catch with Phylactery Lich: Genesis Wave puts Phylactery Lich and Humility onto the battlefield simultaneously, so Humility is already on the battlefield and applying to Phylactery Lich at the moment Phylactery Lich is there. Phylactery Lich therefore has lost "As this creature enters, put a phylactery counter on an artifact you control" (and "Indestructible," and its sacrifice trigger) under the same layer-6 application [613.1f]. The rules provided here don't fully spell out how an "as this creature enters" replacement effect interacts with an ability-removing static effect that begins applying in the same event, so I can't settle that half definitively from this context — but if that ability does apply, Tatterkite is a legal recipient (it's an artifact you control, and it no longer refuses counters).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming both permanents hit the battlefield in the same Genesis Wave resolution, simultaneously. If instead Phylactery Lich were already on the battlefield and Humility arrived later, the counter would have been placed at the earlier time — and back then Tatterkite still had its ability, so Tatterkite could not have been chosen.

Player count: this interaction is entirely between Ashley's own permanents, so it plays out the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Phylactery Lich and Humility enter the battlefield at the same time. Tatterkite had the ability that prevents it from getting counters immediately before Phylactery Lich entered the battlefield, which is when it matters.

entries.question: Avery controls [The One Ring] and casts [Teferi's Protection] then casts a second The One Ring. What happens at the start of the next turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the phased-out Ring returns, Avery ends up with two Rings so one is put into the graveyard by state-based actions/legend rule before priority, and the triggers (using last‑known information) will cause the appropriate life loss once Teferi's Protection ends.
entries.answer:
Direct answer: at the start of Avery's next turn, both copies of The One Ring phase back in / are present, and then the "legend rule" makes Avery choose one The One Ring to keep and put the other into their graveyard. Teferi's Protection's protection-from-everything and life-total lock also expire at that point.

Step by step, with my timing assumption stated: I'm assuming Avery cast Teferi's Protection and the second The One Ring during a single turn, and that "the start of the next turn" you mean is the beginning of Avery's own next turn (that's when Teferi's Protection's effects end and phased-out permanents return). 

1. Teferi's Protection phases out all permanents Avery controls, including the first The One Ring. Phasing means a permanent is treated as though it doesn't exist while phased out, and Teferi's Protection's own reminder text says those permanents "phase in before you untap during your untap step." Because the first The One Ring doesn't exist while phased out, it doesn't conflict with the newly cast second The One Ring, which enters normally and (since it was cast) gives Avery protection from everything until Avery's next turn.
2. During Avery's untap step, the first The One Ring phases in. Now Avery controls two legendary permanents with the same name, and the legend rule applies as a state-based action, so Avery keeps one and puts the other into the graveyard. Note that both are indestructible, but the legend rule doesn't destroy — it puts the permanent into the graveyard, which indestructible does not stop (compare the note that umbra armor doesn't help "if the 'legend rule' applies to it" — [Spider Umbra ruling #8]).
3. Also at that time, Teferi's Protection's "until your next turn" effects (life total can't change, protection from everything) have ended, and so has the protection from the second The One Ring's enters trigger. So in that turn's upkeep, The One Ring's "lose 1 life for each burden counter" trigger will actually cost Avery life. (While Avery's life total couldn't change, such loss did nothing.)

Caveat on grounding: the provided rules context does not include the numbered legend-rule rule itself; the analogous state-based actions given are the "world rule" [704.5k] and the Role rule [704.5y]/[303.7a], plus [702.26p] on phasing being redundant. My statement of the legend rule rests on Teferi's Protection's and The One Ring's card text plus [Spider Umbra ruling #8]'s reference to it. Also note [514.2]: damage marked on phased-out permanents is still removed at cleanup, which doesn't matter for artifacts here.

If instead you meant the start of the very next turn and that turn belongs to an opponent, nothing happens yet: Avery's permanents stay phased out and keep not existing, so no legend-rule choice occurs until Avery's own untap step. In a two-player game the next turn is the opponent's; at a multiplayer table there may be several turns before Avery's untap step, and during all of them Avery has protection from everything and an unchangeable life total, with only the second The One Ring visible on the battlefield.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The One Ring will phase back in during the untap step. Then all triggered abilities will go onto the stack, then before Avery gets priority they will have to sacrifice a The One Ring to state-based actions. When the triggers resolve the trigger affiliated with the sacrificed The One Ring will use last known information to determine how many counters were on it, and how much life Avery should lose.

entries.question: Amaya controls [Dralnu, Lich Lord], [Furnace of Rath] and six [Snow-Covered Forest]s. Nico casts [Incinerate] targeting Dralnu, Lich Lord. If Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath, how many other permanents will they need to sacrifice?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling as the reference — Amaya's choice of replacement-order makes it either 2 other permanents (Dralnu first) or 5 other permanents (Furnace first).
entries.answer:
Direct answer: if the damage is doubled first, Amaya sacrifices six permanents total, so five permanents besides Furnace of Rath. Note that sacrificing Furnace of Rath doesn't shrink the number — the doubling was already locked in when the replacement applied.

Why: Incinerate would deal 3 damage to Dralnu, Lich Lord. Furnace of Rath changes that to 6 damage, and Dralnu, Lich Lord's own text ("If damage would be dealt to Dralnu, sacrifice that many permanents instead") converts 6 damage into sacrificing 6 permanents. Sacrificing means moving a permanent you control from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard ([701.21a], [Sacrifice]); Furnace of Rath counts as one of those six, so five more permanents (e.g. five of the six Snow-Covered Forests) must go. Sacrificing is not destruction, so regeneration-type effects can't save them ([701.21a]).

Important timing/ordering caveat: both Furnace of Rath and Dralnu, Lich Lord are damage-replacement effects applying to the same damage event, and the provided rules context does not include the rule governing who orders multiple applicable replacement effects. If instead Dralnu, Lich Lord's replacement is applied first, the 3 damage is replaced by sacrificing 3 permanents and there is no damage left for Furnace of Rath to double — that would be 2 other permanents besides Furnace of Rath. I've answered the reading your question implies (doubling applied, 6 sacrifices).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: Amaya is the one sacrificing her own permanents either way, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Two or five, Amaya's choice.

Both Dralnu, Lich Lord and Furnace of Rath have replacement effects that modify how the game handles damage that is being dealt to Dralnu, Lich Lord. As Amaya is the controller of the affected object, Amaya will choose which order to apply the replacement effects in. If Amaya chooses to apply Dralnu, Lich Lord's effect first, the 3 damage will be converted into sacrificing three permanents, and Furnace of Rath will no longer apply to that event since there's no longer any damage being dealt. If they chooses to apply Furnace of Rath first, then the three damage will be doubled to six damage, and then will be replaced by sacrificing six permanents.

Whether Amaya chooses to sacrifice Furnace of Rath or not is irrelevant, as all replacement effects are applied to the event before anything is actually sacrificed.

entries.question: Aubrey and Arely are playing 2HG. Aubrey attacks with [Coral Commando] and Arely casts [Flash Conscription] to gain control of Coral Commando after it's been declared as an attacker in the declare attackers step. Is it still attacking?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that gaining control of the attacking creature removes it from combat (per 506.4a), so Coral Commando is no longer attacking.
entries.answer:
No — Coral Commando stops being an attacking creature the moment Flash Conscription resolves and Arely gains control of it.

A permanent is removed from combat if its controller changes, and a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4a]. Flash Conscription's control-change effect therefore takes Coral Commando out of combat entirely; it also untaps Coral Commando and gives it haste, but that doesn't put it back into combat. No combat damage will be dealt by Coral Commando this combat unless some other effect states it's attacking again.

A couple of related points:
- Coral Commando is still considered to have been declared as an attacker for the purposes of anything that already triggered on attackers being declared [508.3]; removal from combat doesn't undo that historical fact, but ongoing 'is attacking' checks fail.
- Nothing here is a 'reselect what it's attacking' effect [508.7], nor an effect that states a creature is attacking [508.4], so Coral Commando is simply out of combat.

Two-Headed Giant note: 2HG uses shared team turns, where the active team declares attackers as one combined attack [805.10b]. That doesn't change the outcome. If Arely is Aubrey's teammate on the attacking team, the controller of Coral Commando still changed, so 506.4a still removes it from combat. If Arely is an opposing player, the same rule applies. Either way Coral Commando is no longer attacking.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Flash Conscription resolves during the declare attackers step, after attackers were declared and before combat damage. If instead it somehow resolved before attackers were declared, Coral Commando would simply never have been declared as an attacker by Aubrey [508.1c].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature that changes controllers is removed from combat. Even though Aubrey and Arely are on the same team and are both allowed to be attacking with creatures, they are different players and therefore Arely gaining control of Aubrey's creature still qualifies as a control change.

entries.question: Nicolas controls [Razorfield Thresher], [Lake of the Dead], and [Veinfire Borderpost]. Aubrey controls [Omniscience] and casts [Casualties of War], choosing Razorfield Thresher as the artifact target and the creature target. Then they cast [Radiate], targeting Casualties of War. What will be destroyed after all spells and abilities have resolved?
entries.reason: The candidate is wrong — both Razorfield Thresher and Veinfire Borderpost are destroyed: Radiate will create a copy that can target Veinfire for the artifact mode (the spell's modes are locked in but copies may choose new legal targets), so more than just the Thresher dies.
entries.answer:
Only Razorfield Thresher is destroyed. Nothing else on the battlefield dies.

Why: Casualties of War is modal, and Aubrey chose two modes ("Destroy target artifact" and "Destroy target creature") both pointing at Razorfield Thresher, an artifact creature. Because both instances of "target" are on the same permanent, the spell targets only a single permanent, so it is a legal choice for Radiate. Razorfield Thresher is simply destroyed once when Casualties of War resolves — the two modes both apply to the same object, exactly as in the Plague Spores example in rule [608.2b], where one permanent chosen for two target instances is affected by the parts of the spell it's legal for.

Radiate then copies Casualties of War "for each other permanent or player the spell could target," with each copy targeting a different one. A copy of this Casualties of War keeps the same two chosen modes, so it needs a permanent that is legal for both "target artifact" and "target creature" — that is, another artifact creature. Lake of the Dead is a land, Veinfire Borderpost is a noncreature artifact, and Omniscience is an enchantment, so none of them qualifies (and players can't be targeted by these modes at all). With no other legal object, Radiate produces no copies and nothing additional is destroyed.

Timing note: I'm assuming Radiate resolves while Casualties of War is still on the stack (as it must be, since Radiate targets a spell). If Razorfield Thresher somehow left the battlefield before Casualties of War resolved, all of its targets would be illegal and Casualties of War would not resolve at all ([608.2b]).

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any player count with only these permanents, but at a larger table Radiate would make one copy for each other artifact creature on the battlefield, destroying each of those too.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Both Razorfield Thresher and Veinfire Borderpost will be destroyed but no other cards will be destroyed. Once Casualties of War is on the stack, it's a spell with modes that have been locked in, so that the only permanents it can target are artifacts and creatures.

entries.question: Amare controls [Psychogenic Probe] and casts [Pain], targeting Nico. They discard a [Progenitus]. Does Psychogenic Probe trigger?
entries.reason: Both conclude Progenitus's replacement effect turns the discard into a reveal-and-shuffle, so Pain causes Nico to shuffle and Psychogenic Probe triggers (dealing 2 damage to Nico).
entries.answer:
Yes — Psychogenic Probe triggers and deals 2 damage to Nico.

Pain makes Nico discard a card. Progenitus's own replacement ability reads "If Progenitus would be put into a graveyard from anywhere, reveal Progenitus and shuffle it into its owner's library instead." That card text overrides the general result of a discard (going to the graveyard), so instead Progenitus is revealed and shuffled into Nico's library. Because the shuffle actually happens, and it happens as a result of a spell (Pain) and an ability (Progenitus's replacement ability), Psychogenic Probe's trigger condition — "Whenever a spell or ability causes a player to shuffle their library" — is met, and it deals 2 damage to Nico, the player who shuffled.

Note that the trigger only exists because the shuffle genuinely occurs; a trigger condition that is prevented or replaced away never triggers ([603.2g]). Here nothing prevents the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers once for that one shuffle. This works the same regardless of whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game: the damage goes to Nico, the player who shuffled, not to Amare.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Progenitus's replacement effect changes the effect of Pain from "Nico discards a card, putting it into their graveyard" to "Nico reveals a card and shuffles it into their library". Pain still caused the shuffle, so Psychogenic Probe triggers.

entries.question: Alonso controls [Spark Double] and casts [Clone]. Alonso would like to have Clone copy Spark Double, then they would like to apply the replacement effect Clone inherited from Spark Double and have it copy Spark Double again. If Alonso has Clone copy Spark Double a total of four times, how many +1/+1 counters will Clone enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Clone enters with one +1/+1 counter and correctly explain that only the last-applied Spark Double copy exception can grant the counter, so prior ones are negated.
entries.answer:
Clone enters the battlefield with exactly one +1/+1 counter, no matter how many times it copies Spark Double.

Why: Spark Double's copy effect is written as "You may have this creature enter as a copy of a creature or planeswalker you control, except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it if it's a creature..." That "except it enters with an additional +1/+1 counter" clause is an additional effect, not a modification of the copiable characteristics. Rule 707.9e says that when a replacement effect generating a copy effect has such an exception, and another copy effect is later applied to that object, the earlier exception's effect simply doesn't happen.

So the chain works like this: Clone's own replacement effect (which has no counter clause) makes Clone a copy of Spark Double. Now Clone has Spark Double's replacement effect, which Alonso applies to copy Spark Double again — that application would grant a counter, but because Alonso then applies yet another copy effect (the newly inherited Spark Double effect) afterward, the earlier one's counter never materializes. Only the very last copy effect applied still has a live exception, and it grants exactly one +1/+1 counter. Repeating this four times, or forty, still yields one counter, since each prior exception is wiped out by the next copy effect.

Note that after the last iteration Clone is a copy of Spark Double, so its printed power/toughness is 0/0 (copiable values, applied in layer 1a per 613.2a and 613.1a); with one +1/+1 counter it will be a 1/1 unless something else copied changes that. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Alonso's own permanents are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Spark Double has a copy effect that includes an exception (entering with a +1/+1 counter). If another copy effect is applied afterwards, the exception from the first effect will not happen.

entries.question: Nickolas controls a [Nyx Herald] enchanted by [Drake Umbra]. Ainsley casts [Fracturing Gust]. How much life do they gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Fracturing Gust only destroys Drake Umbra (Nyx Herald is saved by the replacement effect), so Ainsley gains 2 life.
entries.answer:
Ainsley gains 2 life from this pair of permanents (plus 2 more for each other artifact or enchantment Fracturing Gust destroys anywhere on the battlefield).

Why: Fracturing Gust says "Destroy all artifacts and enchantments. You gain 2 life for each permanent destroyed this way." Both Nyx Herald (an enchantment creature) and Drake Umbra (an enchantment Aura) are hit. But Drake Umbra grants umbra armor: "If enchanted creature would be destroyed, instead remove all damage from it and destroy this Aura." That replacement effect applies to Nyx Herald's destruction, so Nyx Herald is not destroyed at all \u2014 instead damage is removed from it and Drake Umbra is destroyed. Card text like umbra armor overrides the general expectation that everything named by Fracturing Gust dies.

So the only permanent of Nickolas's that Fracturing Gust actually destroys is Drake Umbra, which is one permanent \u2192 2 life. Nyx Herald survives (now unenchanted, so it loses the +3/+3 and flying).

Timing note: Drake Umbra is itself already being destroyed by Fracturing Gust at the same time; the umbra armor replacement doesn't add a second, separately-counted destruction of Drake Umbra, so you don't get 4 life. Either way Nyx Herald is never "destroyed this way" and never contributes life.

This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game \u2014 Fracturing Gust destroys artifacts and enchantments controlled by every player, and Ainsley gains 2 life for each one, so at a larger table the total is usually much higher.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. There are two different instances of "destroy Drake Umbra" attempting to occur, so Ainsley chooses one of them. Only that one takes place, and only one permanent is destroyed.

entries.question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Rescuer Sphinx enters with one counter, contradicting the reference ruling that it enters with two because replacement effects are chosen before the creature actually enters so Corpsejack's doubling still applies.
entries.answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's ability is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters — "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it." An effect that modifies how a permanent enters the battlefield may cause other objects to change zones as part of applying it [614.13b]. So Corpsejack Menace is returned to Avery's hand before Rescuer Sphinx actually enters and before the counter is placed.

Corpsejack Menace's doubling effect ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") only functions while Corpsejack Menace is on the battlefield. Since Avery chose to bounce Corpsejack Menace itself, it is no longer on the battlefield to apply its replacement effect to the single counter Rescuer Sphinx would enter with. Result: one +1/+1 counter, making Rescuer Sphinx a 4/3 flyer.

If Avery had instead returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, the one counter would be doubled to two, and Rescuer Sphinx would enter as a 5/4.

Player count doesn't matter here — this works identically in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since only Avery's own permanents and Avery's own choice are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Avery will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Corpsejack Menace will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.

entries.question: Arabella casts [Mind's Desire]. In response, Neil casts [Lim-Dûl's Vault]. How many copies of Mind's Desire are created when the storm trigger resolves?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes storm only counts spells cast before Mind's Desire, so Lim‑Dûl's Vault cast in response does not add copies.
entries.answer:
Zero copies — assuming Mind's Desire was the first spell cast this turn.

Storm means "When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn" [702.40a]. The key word is *before*: only spells cast earlier in the turn than Mind's Desire count. Neil's Lim-Dûl's Vault was cast in response, i.e. after Mind's Desire was already on the stack, so it does not add a copy no matter when the storm trigger actually resolves.

So the count is simply however many spells (by any player) were cast earlier in that turn before Mind's Desire. If Mind's Desire was the turn's first spell, the storm trigger resolves and makes zero copies; Arabella still resolves the original Mind's Desire (shuffle, exile top card, may play it without paying its mana cost this turn). If, say, two spells had already been cast that turn before Mind's Desire, you'd get two copies, and Lim-Dûl's Vault still wouldn't make it three.

Each copy would be a spell on the stack that wasn't cast, and it copies all decisions made for the original [707.10b]. Mind's Desire has no targets, so the "you may choose new targets" clause of storm is irrelevant here [702.40a].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games: storm counts spells cast before it that turn by *any* player, not just its controller, so opponents' earlier spells in the turn do increase the count — but a spell cast in response afterward never does.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The storm trigger only cares about spells cast before the spell that caused it to trigger.

entries.question: Aubrey casts [Bitter Ordeal], targeting Natasha. At their first opportunity, Aubrey sacrifices their [Westvale Abbey]. How many cards will Aubrey be able to exile from Natasha's library?
entries.reason: The candidate declined to give a definitive ruling—calling the situation ambiguous—whereas the reference states gravestorm counts permanents put into graveyards before the trigger resolves (so the Abbey sacrifice would be counted and Aubrey would exile two cards).
entries.answer:
Short answer: the provided rules don't contain the gravestorm rules needed to settle this cleanly, so I can't fully ground a number.

What I can say from the given material: Bitter Ordeal's own text is "Search target player's library for a card and exile it," so each resolution of Bitter Ordeal (and of each gravestorm copy) exiles exactly one card from Natasha's library, and if Natasha's library is empty or has fewer cards than the total number of resolutions, Aubrey simply finds as many as possible [701.23d], since an effect that attempts the impossible does only as much as possible [609.3].

So the total number of cards exiled equals 1 (for Bitter Ordeal itself) plus the number of gravestorm copies. Determining whether Aubrey's Westvale Abbey, sacrificed after Bitter Ordeal was cast but (presumably) before the gravestorm triggered ability resolves, is counted for gravestorm requires the gravestorm rules and the rules for when a triggered ability's count is determined — neither is in the context I was given. Note also that Westvale Abbey's printed abilities don't themselves sacrifice Westvale Abbey (its third ability sacrifices five creatures to transform it), so the question presupposes some other effect sacrificing it; and the exact timing (before or after the gravestorm trigger resolves) is the crux. If the sacrifice happens in time to be counted, Aubrey exiles 2 cards; if the count was already locked in, Aubrey exiles 1.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more, since Bitter Ordeal targets a single player, Natasha.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2. Gravestorm cares about the number of permanents put into the graveyard before the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Albert controls [Doubling Season] and [Pir, Imaginative Rascal] and activates the +1 ability of [Ajani, Mentor of Heroes]. How many loyalty counters does it gain?
entries.reason: Both conclude the controller orders Pir before Doubling Season to produce four loyalty counters, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Albert chooses the order, so Ajani, Mentor of Heroes gains either 3 or 4 loyalty counters — 4 if he applies Pir, Imaginative Rascal first, 3 if he applies Doubling Season first. He'll almost certainly choose 4.

Why: the +1 puts one loyalty counter on Ajani, Mentor of Heroes. Both Doubling Season ("If an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control, it puts twice that many...") and Pir, Imaginative Rascal ("If one or more counters would be put on a permanent your team controls, that many plus one...") are replacement effects that want to modify that same event. When two or more replacement effects would apply to one event, the affected object's controller picks the order one at a time (rule 616.1g), and each effect only gets one chance to apply — it doesn't re-trigger off its own modification (rule 614.5).

- Pir, Imaginative Rascal first: 1 + 1 = 2, then Doubling Season: 2 × 2 = 4.
- Doubling Season first: 1 × 2 = 2, then Pir, Imaginative Rascal: 2 + 1 = 3.

So Albert should apply Pir, Imaginative Rascal before Doubling Season for 4 loyalty counters. (The same math applies to the three +1/+1 counters that ability distributes when it resolves: each targeted creature's counters get the same replacement treatment, chosen per event.)

I'm assuming Albert controls both permanents when the ability is activated, and that both were already on the battlefield at that time. This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — only Albert, as the controller of the affected permanent, makes the ordering choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Four.

Activating a planeswalker ability includes paying the loyalty cost, which in this case means adding one loyalty counter. Doubling Season only replaces effects, which are the result of a spell or ability. However Pir, Imaginative Rascal replaces the original one loyalty counter with two, which Doubling Season can then replace with doubling the additional loyalty counters, resulting in a total of four.

entries.question: Ainsley activates [Priest of Forgotten Gods]'s ability, but doesn't choose a target for the first part. Can Nickolas respond to the ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the activated ability goes on the stack (is not a mana ability) and can be responded to even if zero targets are chosen, so Nickolas may respond.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nickolas can respond normally. Choosing zero targets doesn't stop Priest of Forgotten Gods's activated ability from going on the stack; it sits there like any other activated ability, and players receive priority and may cast spells or activate abilities in response before it resolves.

Why: Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability reads "Any number of target players each lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice. You add {B}{B} and draw a card." "Any number of target players" permits zero targets. Rule 115.6 says such an ability is still said to require targets, but it is only actually "targeted" if one or more targets were chosen — so with zero players chosen, the ability simply isn't a targeted ability. That affects things like effects that say "counter target spell or ability that targets you," but it does not remove the ability from the stack or deny anyone priority.

Because Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability targets, it is not a mana ability, even though it adds {B}{B}. Only mana abilities skip the stack and resolve immediately without being respondable (rule 605.3b); this ability does use the stack, so Nickolas gets a window to respond. Note Nickolas can respond by, for example, removing Priest of Forgotten Gods — but the ability still resolves, since the cost ({T}, sacrificing two other creatures) was already paid.

On resolution with zero target players, no one loses 2 life or sacrifices a creature, and Ainsley still adds {B}{B} and draws a card.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same regardless of player count; with more than two players Ainsley could have chosen several target players ("any number"), and each chosen player would lose 2 life and sacrifice a creature of their choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. One of the qualifications for being a mana ability is that the ability doesn't require a target. Priest of Forgotten Gods's ability is still considered to require targets even if zero targets were chosen for it.

entries.question: Analia controls [Volrath's Shapeshifter] and [Muldrotha, the Gravetide], and the top card of their graveyard is [Grid Monitor]. Can Analia cast the Grid Monitor?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Volrath's Shapeshifter's copied "You can't cast creature spells" prohibition prevents Analia from casting Grid Monitor despite Muldrotha's permission, so they reach the same ruling.
entries.answer:

The +1/+1 counter Slip Out the Back put on it is still there, so it's a 2/2.

Timing of the return: because Slip Out the Back phases it out "until its controller's next turn," a second one-shot effect phases it in at that point ([610.4], [610.4a]) rather than via the normal untap-step phasing turn-based action ([502.1], [703.4a]).

Assumed order: the activation happened first and Slip Out the Back was cast while that ability was still on the stack (as stated). If instead the {S}{S} ability had fully resolved before Slip Out the Back resolved, Ascendant Spirit would already be a Spirit Warrior with base 2/3 and would phase back in that way, as a 3/4 with the counter — those changes last indefinitely and phasing doesn't undo them.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since only Avery's own permanent and untap step are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It will be a 2/2 and not a Warrior. When Ascendant Spirit's ability resolves it's phased out and won't be affected.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Parallel Lives] and a [Caldera Hellion]. They cast [Rite of Replication] targeting the Caldera Hellion. Can Aspen apply the devour replacement effect before the Parallel Lives replacement effect, sacrificing 1 creature to have each token enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Parallel Lives' replacement applies first (doubling the tokens), then each token's Devour choices are made individually, so sacrificing one creature can only apply to one token.
entries.answer:
No. Parallel Lives' replacement effect must be applied first, and even then a single sacrificed creature can only be counted once.

Why Parallel Lives goes first: when one replacement effect applies to an event and another applies to an event contained within it, the outer effect must be chosen first [616.1g]. Creating a token is the outer event, and the token entering the battlefield is contained within it, so Parallel Lives ("If an effect would create one or more tokens under your control, it creates twice that many of those tokens instead") applies before any devour effect on the tokens as they enter. Devour is a replacement effect that modifies how the permanent enters the battlefield [702.82c], so it can't be chosen ahead of Parallel Lives.

So Rite of Replication (uncast without its {5} kicker) creates one token copy of Caldera Hellion, doubled by Parallel Lives to two tokens; kicked, five becomes ten. Each token is a copy of Caldera Hellion and thus has Devour 1, and each token's devour choice is made before it enters [614.12a], in either order [616.1g].

The key limit: the same object can't be chosen to change zones more than once when applying replacement effects that modify how one or more permanents enter the battlefield [614.13b]. So sacrificing one creature satisfies devour for only one of the tokens — that token enters with one +1/+1 counter, and the other token(s) enter with zero unless you sacrifice additional, different creatures. Also, you can't sacrifice any of the Caldera Hellion tokens themselves, since objects entering the battlefield at the same time can't be chosen [614.13a].

Note too that the original Caldera Hellion on the battlefield is a legal sacrifice for devour (it isn't entering), and each token's "When this creature enters, it deals 3 damage to each creature" triggers will go on the stack after all tokens have entered.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player or multiplayer game, since all the choices here belong to Aspen (APNAP ordering under [616.1] only matters when multiple players choose simultaneously).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. There are two replacement effects trying to apply to the original event of creating a Caldera Hellion: Caldera Hellion's own effect and Parallel Lives's effect. Caldera Hellion's effect applies to it entering the battlefield however, while Parallel Lives's effect applies to it being created, so Parallel Lives's effect must be applied first. After that is applied the original Caldera Hellion's effect doesn't exist anymore, but each of the new Caldera Hellions entering the battlefield has its own effect, which can now be applied individually.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Exotic Orchard]. Nikolas controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
entries.reason: The candidate incorrectly concludes Exotic Orchard produces no mana by ignoring that Exotic Orchard's check includes triggered abilities (so Crumbling Vestige's ETB trigger that can add one mana of any color means Exotic Orchard can produce any color).
entries.answer:
Exotic Orchard produces no mana at all.

Exotic Orchard's ability is "{T}: Add one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land Nikolas controls is Crumbling Vestige, whose activated mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana specifically — colorless is not a color, so Crumbling Vestige could produce no *color* of mana. Crumbling Vestige's other mana-producing ability ("When this land enters, add one mana of any color") is a triggered ability tied to it entering the battlefield; it isn't an ability that would resolve at the time Aubrey taps Exotic Orchard, so it doesn't define a color for the "could produce" check either (106.7 asks what an ability of that permanent would produce if it were to resolve at that time).

With no color definable, the type of mana Exotic Orchard would produce is undefined, and an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces no mana instead (106.5, and the Exotic Orchard example in 106.7). Aubrey still taps Exotic Orchard and gets nothing.

Multiplayer note: Exotic Orchard checks lands controlled by any opponent, not just one. In a two-player game Nikolas's Crumbling Vestige is the whole picture; at a table with more opponents, any color that any other opponent's land could produce would also be available to Exotic Orchard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Any color. Exotic Orchard checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

entries.question: Azariah, Beckham, and Caelan are playing a multiplayer game. Beckham controls [Stalking Leonin]. Azariah casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Beckham's next turn. After Beckham begins their turn, can Azariah see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Azariah can see the secret choice made when Stalking Leonin entered, which contradicts the reference ruling that that choice is not visible to the controller-of-player and thus the answers differ.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Azariah's Worst Fears effect begins and Azariah controls Beckham for Beckham's turn, Azariah can see which opponent Beckham secretly chose for Stalking Leonin.

Why: Worst Fears reads "You control target player during that player's next turn... (You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them.)" Rule 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it's visible to both that player and the controller of the player. The secret choice recorded for Stalking Leonin is information about an object in the game (Stalking Leonin, a permanent Beckham controls) that Beckham can see, so Azariah sees it too. (By contrast, 723.4 keeps information about cards *outside* the game private to the controlled player — that exception doesn't apply here.)

Practical consequences during that turn: under 723.5b Azariah makes all choices and decisions Beckham is allowed to make, including whether to activate Stalking Leonin's "Reveal the player you chose" ability — though note that ability only exiles an attacking creature if it's controlled by the chosen player, and on Beckham's own turn Beckham is unlikely to be attacked. Control of objects doesn't change: Stalking Leonin is still Beckham's permanent (723.3), and Beckham remains the active player. Beckham also still makes their own non-game decisions and personal choices (723.5b, 723.8).

Multiplayer note: this is already a three-player game, and nothing changes with more players — the chosen opponent could be Azariah or Caelan, and either way Azariah sees it. If your table uses the limited range of influence option, the secret choice of an opponent must be a player within Beckham's range (801.5a); with a normal unlimited range that's no restriction here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Stalking Leonin already entered and the secret choice was made before Beckham's controlled turn began. If instead Stalking Leonin enters during the turn Azariah controls Beckham, Azariah makes that secret choice themselves (723.5b) and obviously knows it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Beckham. Azariah can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

entries.question: Angela controls [Mirror Gallery] and two [Sakashima the Impostor]s. One is a copy of their [Master of the Hunt]; the other is copying a wolf token created by Master of the Hunt. They attack with all four creatures. What are the possible bands that Angela may declare?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude no bands are possible because only the token is named Wolves of the Hunt and the Sakashima copies are not, so there aren't two eligible creatures to form a band.
entries.answer:
Angela can't declare any bands at all — all four creatures attack as individual, unbanded attackers.

Why: Rule 702.22c gives exactly two ways to form an attacking band.

1) The plain-banding way: one or more attacking creatures with the banding keyword, plus up to one attacking creature without banding (even one that has "bands with other"). None of Angela's four attackers has plain banding. Master of the Hunt has no banding — it only creates tokens; the Sakashima the Impostor that copied Master of the Hunt likewise has no banding (copying doesn't grant one, and Master of the Hunt's granted ability lives on the tokens it makes). So this route is unavailable.

2) The "bands with other [quality]" way: one or more attacking [quality] creatures that have "bands with other [quality]" plus any number of other attacking [quality] creatures. Here the quality is "creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." The Wolves of the Hunt token qualifies — it is named Wolves of the Hunt and has "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt." But it is the only creature on Angela's side with that name, and a band needs at least two creatures, so it has nothing to band with. The Sakashima the Impostor copying the Wolves of the Hunt token does have the ability "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt," but Sakashima the Impostor's copy effect keeps its name as Sakashima the Impostor, so it is not itself a creature named Wolves of the Hunt. It therefore fails both halves of 702.22c: it isn't a [quality] creature with the "bands with other" ability, and it isn't another [quality] creature that could be swept into a band.

Mirror Gallery matters only in that its text ("The 'legend rule' doesn't apply") lets Angela keep two legendary Sakashima the Impostors plus a legendary-copied Master of the Hunt on the battlefield at once; it has no effect on banding.

Also note that banding doesn't share abilities between attackers (702.22g), so the Sakashima the Impostor copying Master of the Hunt can't lend anything here either. Had a band been legal, every member would have had to attack the same player, planeswalker, or battle (702.22d, 802.3b) — that restriction is the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer, where the attacking player chooses a defending player per attacker (802.3b). Attackers and any bands are declared as part of the declare attackers turn-based action (508.1e).

If Angela made a second Wolves of the Hunt token before attacking, then the two real Wolves of the Hunt tokens could band together (the Sakashima the Impostor copy still couldn't join).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No bands can be declared. The only creature on the battlefield named "Wolves of the Hunt" is the token, so it cannot declare itself as in a band with anything else. The Sakashima the Impostor with "bands with other creatures named Wolves of the Hunt" is not itself named "Wolves of the Hunt", so it cannot declare itself as in a band with the token.

entries.question: Avery controls a Germ token that's equipped with [Barbed Bloodletter]. Nadia controls two [Teferi's Curse]s, one on the Germ, the other on the Barbed Bloodletter. During Avery's untap step, which permanents will phase out? Which of these will phase back in?
entries.reason: Both answers state that all four permanents phase out during Avery's untap step and then all phase back in together on Avery's next untap step, with the Auras remaining attached.
entries.answer:
All four permanents phase out during Avery's untap step, and none of them phase back in during that same untap step — they all phase in during Avery's *next* untap step.

Detail:

1. **Phasing out (this untap step).** Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step: before the active player untaps, every phased-in permanent with phasing that player controls phases out, and every phased-out permanent that player controlled when it phased out phases in — all simultaneously [702.26a] [502.1] [703.4a].
 - The Germ token has phasing (granted by Nadia's Teferi's Curse attached to it) and is controlled by Avery, so it phases out directly.
 - Barbed Bloodletter also has phasing (granted by the second Teferi's Curse attached to Barbed Bloodletter) and is controlled by Avery, so it too phases out directly.
 - Both copies of Teferi's Curse phase out "indirectly" — Auras attached to a permanent that phases out phase out at the same time, even though Nadia controls them [702.26g].

2. **Nothing phases in this untap step**, since nothing of Avery's was already phased out.

3. **Phasing back in.** On Avery's next untap step, every permanent that phased out under Avery's control phases in: the Germ token and Barbed Bloodletter [702.26a] [502.1]. The two Teferi's Curses phased out indirectly, so they don't phase in on their own (and won't phase in on Nadia's untap step) — each phases in along with the permanent it's attached to [702.26g], which is the same moment. Barbed Bloodletter, having phased out directly, phases in attached to the Germ token if that token is still on the battlefield [702.26i].

Notes: phasing out isn't a zone change or change of control, so no leaves-the-battlefield or unattach triggers occur, the token keeps existing while phased out, and counters stay on it [702.26d] [702.26j]. If some effect makes Avery skip their untap step, the phasing event simply doesn't happen that turn [702.26m].

This works identically in a two-player or multiplayer game, with one multiplayer caveat: if the controller of a phased-out permanent leaves the game, that permanent may leave the game or be exiled, and a permanent that phased out under a departed player's control phases in during the next untap step after that player's next turn would have begun [702.26n].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All 4 permanents will phase out and phase back in in Ari's next untap step. Barbed Bloodletter and both Teferi's Curses will still be attached to the permanents they were attached to previously. Phasing doesn't cause tokens to cease to exist or unattach permanents from other permanents.

entries.question: Alessandra controls [Sheoldred, the Apocalypse]. During their main phase, they cast [Day's Undoing]. How much life does each player gain/lose?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Sheoldred's triggers are nullified by Day's Undoing ending the turn, so no one gains or loses life.
entries.answer:
Short answer: nobody gains or loses any life (assuming Alessandra casts Day's Undoing on their own turn, as stated).

Why: Day's Undoing has each player shuffle hand and graveyard into their library and draw seven cards. Sheoldred, the Apocalypse's abilities do trigger on those draws \,, you gain 2 life" for each of Alessandra's seven draws, and "whenever an opponent draws a card, they lose 2 life" for each opponent's seven draws \, so 14 life would be gained by Alessandra and 14 lost by each opponent. However, those are triggered abilities: they wait to be put on the stack, and Day's Undoing is still resolving. Because it's Alessandra's turn, Day's Undoing then says "end the turn," whose reminder text reads "Exile all spells and abilities from the stack, including this card." The Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers are exiled along with everything else and never resolve, so no life is gained or lost.

Timing caveat: if instead Day's Undoing were somehow cast during an opponent's turn (it's a sorcery, so this would require an effect allowing it), the "end the turn" clause would not apply, the Sheoldred, the Apocalypse triggers would resolve normally, and Alessandra would gain 14 life while each opponent lost 14 life.

Multiplayer: with more than two players, every opponent draws seven, so in the "turn doesn't end" case each opponent separately loses 14 life; in the actual case (Alessandra's own turn) it's still zero for everyone. In a Two-Headed Giant game, life gained or lost happens to each player individually but is applied to that team's shared life total [810.9], and if an effect says a player can't gain or lose life, no one on that team can [810.9g][810.9h].

One limitation: the numbered rule governing exactly how "end the turn" handles abilities that triggered during resolution was not included in the context; the conclusion above rests on Day's Undoing's own printed text, which overrides the general expectation that triggers go on the stack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. The players first draw seven cards each, triggering Sheoldred, the Apocalypse fourteen times. Then Alessandra ends the turn, which nullifies those triggers before they're even put onto the stack.

entries.question: It is currently day and Adonis controls [Lazotep Convert] (the back face of [Invasion of Amonkhet]), which is a copy of [Kessig Naturalist]. What happens if it becomes night?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Lazotep Convert will not transform when it becomes night because it’s back face up and daybound only causes a transform if the permanent is front face up.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens — Adonis's Lazotep Convert does not transform when it becomes night.

Why: Lazotep Convert is the back face of the double-faced card Invasion of Amonkhet, so the permanent is physically back face up. Copying Kessig Naturalist gives it Kessig Naturalist's copiable text, including daybound, but daybound only says "As it becomes night, if this permanent is front face up, transform it" [702.145b], and the ongoing check in [702.145c] likewise only applies to a permanent that is front face up with daybound while it's night. Lazotep Convert is back face up, so neither the "as it becomes night" trigger-like static ability nor the continuous check does anything. It also doesn't have nightbound (Kessig Naturalist's front face has daybound, not nightbound), so [702.145e]/[702.145f] don't apply either. Daybound additionally says the permanent can't transform except due to its daybound ability [702.145b], so no other effect will flip it.

Day/night itself still behaves normally: the game changes designation during the untap step based on the previous turn's active player's spellcasting [502.2], [731.2], [731.2a], [731.2b]. Note also that because Adonis controls a permanent with daybound, if the game had no designation it would become day [702.145d]; here it is already day, and once the game has a designation it always has exactly one [731.1].

Multiplayer: the rules given for the day/night check are worded around "the previous turn's active player," so they work the same with more than two players (with a modification only for shared team turns) [731.2a], [731.2b]; Lazotep Convert's non-transformation is unaffected by player count.

Timing note: I'm assuming Lazotep Convert is already on the battlefield as a copy of Kessig Naturalist when night arrives. If instead it were entering the battlefield while it's night, the "enters transformed" part of daybound applies only to a permanent represented by a double-faced card and would try to put it onto the battlefield with its other face — Invasion of Amonkhet, a Siege battle, not an instant or sorcery — so unlike the sorcery-back case described in [712.13a] it would not be put into the graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Lazotep Convert will be a copy of Kessig Naturalist. As it becomes night, it will not transform and remain a copy of Kessig Naturalist. Lazotep Convert will only copy the front face of Kessig Naturalist and does not copy its status. When it becomes night, it will not transform because a daybound permanent will only transform as it becomes night if it is front face up. ([702.145b])

entries.question: Adelina's [Fireblade Charger] dies, and Nasir responds with [Thwart the Enemy]. Is the damage prevented?
entries.reason: The reference says the outcome is unclear/ambiguous, while the candidate gives a definitive ruling that the damage is not prevented, so they do not reach the same conclusion.
entries.answer:
No — Thwart the Enemy does not prevent that damage. Once Fireblade Charger has died, it's a card in Adelina's graveyard, not a creature Adelina controls on the battlefield, so its death-trigger damage isn't "damage dealt by creatures your opponents control."

Why: Thwart the Enemy's effect is a prevention shield from a resolved spell that applies to damage from sources with a certain property (a creature controlled by one of Nasir's opponents). When the source would actually deal the damage, the shield rechecks the source's properties; if they no longer match, the damage isn't prevented and the shield isn't used up [609.7b, 615.9, 615.2]. At the time Fireblade Charger's triggered ability resolves and deals damage equal to its power, the source is Fireblade Charger as it last existed on the battlefield — but it is no longer a creature on the battlefield that Adelina controls, so the property check fails.

Timing note: I'm assuming Nasir cast Thwart the Enemy after Fireblade Charger died (in response to the death trigger), which is the reading in the question. Prevention effects must exist before the damage event, so casting it then is legal timing-wise [615.4] — the problem is the source check, not the timing. If Nasir had instead cast Thwart the Enemy earlier in the turn while Fireblade Charger was still on the battlefield, the answer would be the same, because the shield still rechecks the source's properties at the moment damage would be dealt [609.7b].

Terminology: "prevent" means the damage simply never happens; if all of it is prevented, abilities that trigger on damage being dealt don't trigger [615.1a, 615.6, 603.2g]. Here nothing is prevented, so Fireblade Charger's damage is dealt in full to the chosen target.

Multiplayer: no difference. "Creatures your opponents control" covers every opponent's creatures, so whether it's just Nasir and Adelina or a larger table, Fireblade Charger's post-death damage still isn't prevented.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Unclear. Fireblade Charger is not currently a creature on the battlefield, but the game uses its last known information to determine how the damage is dealt. If Fireblade Charger only applies to objects that are creatures, like how Biomantic Mastery only counts creatures that actually exist on the battlefield, it won't be prevented. But if Fireblade Charger checks the source of damage to see whether it's a creature, it will be able to identify the damage as coming from a creature. The intention is probably the latter, but Wizards has not clarified.

entries.question: Aminah casts a [Show and Tell]. As it resolves, Aminah chooses to put a [Haru-Onna] onto the battlefield and Nico chooses to put a [Domestication] onto the battlefield enchanting Haru-Onna. Who controls the enters-the-battlefield ability of Haru-Onna?
entries.reason: The reference states the scenario is impossible because an Aura must target a permanent already on the battlefield, whereas the candidate assumes both enter simultaneously and gives Nico control of Haru-Onna’s ETB trigger.
entries.answer:
Nico controls Haru-Onna's enters-the-battlefield trigger, so Nico draws the card.

Why: Show and Tell puts both cards onto the battlefield simultaneously as it resolves. Haru-Onna would enter under Aminah's control by default (110.2a), and Domestication enters under Nico's control attached to Haru-Onna. But Domestication's "You control enchanted creature" is a continuous control-changing effect, applied in layer 2 (613.1b), and it applies immediately as both permanents exist on the battlefield. So at the moment Haru-Onna is on the battlefield, its controller is Nico.

Haru-Onna's ability ("When this creature enters, draw a card") triggers on that event, and a triggered ability is controlled by the player who controlled its source at the time it triggered (113.8, 603.3a, 109.4b). Since Nico controls Haru-Onna at that time, Nico puts the trigger on the stack and Nico draws the card. Note that an Aura's controller and the enchanted creature's controller are separate matters (303.4e); here Nico happens to be both.

Timing note: I'm assuming Domestication was put onto the battlefield attached to Haru-Onna simultaneously with Haru-Onna, as Show and Tell resolves. If instead Domestication somehow arrived later (e.g., a separately cast Aura after Haru-Onna was already on the battlefield), Haru-Onna's enters trigger would have already triggered under Aminah's control, and Aminah would draw the card; later gaining control of Haru-Onna would not change the controller of that already-triggered ability.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table \-- control of the trigger simply follows whoever controls Haru-Onna the instant it enters.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nico must choose a permanent that is already on the battlefield for the Domestication to enchant. They can't choose a permanent that is entering at the same time.

entries.question:
Amani controls a [Founding the Third Path], and its third ability is resolving. Amani chooses to cast a [Fatal Push] from their graveyard. Amani currently does not have Revolt.
Can Amani choose to target [Skyhunter Patrol] with Fatal Push? Will Skyhunter Patrol be destroyed by Fatal Push?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly says targeting is legal but incorrectly concludes Skyhunter Patrol won't be destroyed — the saga's sacrifice SBAs give Amani Revolt before Fatal Push resolves, so the creature will be destroyed.
entries.answer:
Yes, Amani can legally target Skyhunter Patrol with Fatal Push — but Skyhunter Patrol will not be destroyed.

Why targeting is legal: Fatal Push says "Destroy target creature if it has mana value 2 or less." The only targeting restriction is "target creature" — the mana value clause is a condition on the destruction effect, not part of the target requirement. Skyhunter Patrol is a creature permanent on the battlefield, so it is a legal target (115.2). Nothing about its mana value of 4 makes it an illegal choice.

Why nothing happens: when the copy of Fatal Push resolves, it checks that Skyhunter Patrol is still a legal target; it is, so Fatal Push resolves (608.2b). It then applies its effect, which only destroys the creature if Skyhunter Patrol's mana value is 2 or less. Skyhunter Patrol's mana cost is {2}{W}{W}, so its mana value is 4. Without Revolt (no permanent left the battlefield under Amani's control this turn), the alternative "4 or less" threshold doesn't apply, so Fatal Push resolves and does nothing. Skyhunter Patrol survives.

A note on the Founding the Third Path chapter III: it exiles the Fatal Push card from Amani's graveyard, creates a copy, and Amani may cast that copy — targets for the copy of Fatal Push are chosen as it's cast, at which point Skyhunter Patrol is a valid choice. Also, targeting Skyhunter Patrol counts as committing a crime if Skyhunter Patrol is controlled by an opponent (700.13); this is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

If Amani did somehow enable Revolt before the copy of Fatal Push resolved, the 4-or-less threshold would apply and Skyhunter Patrol would be destroyed.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes Amani can target Skyhunter Patrol, and it will be destroyed by Fatal Push.

Fatal Push does not check for the target's mana value when put on the stack, so Amani is allowed to target Skyhunter Patrol.

Amani will put Fatal Push on the stack as part of the resolution of Founding the Third Path's third chapter. Once the ability is done resolving, SBAs are checked and the saga is sacrificed. In particular this means that Amani will have Revolt when Fatal Push resolves, thus Skyhunter Patrol will get destroyed.

entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Analia controls both permanents, with Lay Claim taking control of the aura first so Corrupted Conscience then grants control of the creature.
entries.answer:
Analia ends up controlling both.

Corrupted Conscience: Analia. Lay Claim reads "You control enchanted permanent," and it's enchanting Nico's Corrupted Conscience, so Analia (Lay Claim's controller) gains control of Corrupted Conscience. Control-changing effects like this are applied in layer 2 [613.1b].

Bane Alley Blackguard: Analia. Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature," and "you" means Corrupted Conscience's controller. Once Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, its control-changing effect now grants Bane Alley Blackguard to Analia instead of Nico. An Aura's controller is tracked separately from the enchanted object's controller, and changing control of one doesn't automatically change control of the other [303.4e] — but here the change flows because Corrupted Conscience's own text points at whoever currently controls it, and both effects are applied together in layer 2 [613.1b]. Note also that Bane Alley Blackguard is Analia's card, but that's incidental: ownership doesn't determine control [110.2b]. Even if Analia weren't the owner, she'd control it via Corrupted Conscience.

One side note: Nico losing control of Bane Alley Blackguard is the kind of event that "leaves the battlefield"-style or "loses control" triggers look back in time for [603.10d], so any such triggered abilities would still see Nico as its controller at that moment.

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players. (If Analia later leaves a multiplayer game, Lay Claim leaves with her and Corrupted Conscience would revert to Nico's control, which would in turn hand Bane Alley Blackguard back to Nico [800.4a].)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. Then the actions — the cards actually being put onto the battlefield — happen simultaneously.

4. If both players' entering permanents had "as it enters" choices at the same time, those choices are likewise made in APNAP order (616.1f, 101.4).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the question as asking about the color choice for Hall of Triumph, not the choice of which card to reveal. If you meant the latter, the answer flips — as active player Asher picks the card first, blind to Noa's pick.

Multiplayer: with more than two players the same structure holds; the active player chooses a card first, then each other player in turn order, and all cards enter simultaneously, so the color choice for Hall of Triumph is made with every other player's entering permanent visible.

entries.question: Avery controls [Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher] and Natalie controls [Verity Circle] and [Koskun Falls]. Avery attacks Natalie with Vhal, Candlekeep Researcher, and then taps it to pay for the cost required by Koskun Falls. Will Natalie's Verity Circle trigger?

entries.question: Nico controls [Platinum Emperion]. Alexandra attacks with [Hopeful Eidolon], which Nico doesn't block. Does Alexandra gain life?

Why: Hopeful Eidolon is a 1/1 with lifelink, and it's unblocked, so it deals 1 combat damage to Nico. Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source's controller to gain that much life, in addition to whatever else the damage does [702.15b, 120.3f]. The two results are separate parts of the same damage event: the damage to Nico would make Nico lose 1 life [120.3a], and separately Alexandra gains 1 life [120.4d]. Platinum Emperion's text "Your life total can't change" applies only to its controller, Nico, so Nico's life total stays where it is, but that has no bearing on Alexandra's life gain [119.3].

Note that the life gain depends on damage actually being dealt — if the combat damage to Nico were prevented entirely, no damage would be dealt and Alexandra would gain nothing. Platinum Emperion doesn't prevent damage; it just stops Nico's life total from changing, so the damage is still dealt and lifelink still applies.

This reasoning is the same at a multiplayer table: Platinum Emperion restricts only its controller's life total, and Hopeful Eidolon's lifelink credits life to Alexandra regardless of which opponent is the defending player. entries.question: Ari casts a [Hero of Oxid Ridge]. In response, Nixon casts [Hallow], targeting the Hero of Oxid Ridge. When Ari attacks with the Hero of Oxid Ridge that turn, will the damage be prevented?

If instead Nixon had cast a prevention spell targeting the creature *permanent* after it resolved (a different card, since Hallow only targets spells), that shield could prevent its combat damage, and if all the damage were prevented, abilities that trigger on damage being dealt wouldn't trigger [603.2g].

This analysis is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer, with one multiplayer caveat: a prevention effect can only affect sources, permanents, and players within its controller's range of influence [801.13b]. entries.question: Ariel controls [Mycosynth Lattice]. Nora controls [Kaslem's Strider] enchanted with [Spirit Away]. Ariel casts [Opportunistic Dragon] and takes control of Spirit Away. What will happen after Opportunistic Dragon's ability resolves?

entries.question: Atlas attacks with [Pristine Angel], and Nico targets it with [Cephalid Snitch] before blockers. After combat, Atlas casts a spell, untapping Pristine Angel. Once untapped, can Nico target it with [Mob]?

Yes — Nico can target Pristine Angel with Mob, assuming all of this happens in the same turn.

Attacking tapped Pristine Angel, so it had no protection at all when Cephalid Snitch was sacrificed. Cephalid Snitch's ability reads "Target creature loses protection from black until end of turn" — that's a continuous effect lasting for the rest of the turn, and it keeps applying even after Pristine Angel becomes untapped again. So when Atlas casts a spell and uses Pristine Angel's "Whenever you cast a spell, you may untap this creature" trigger, Pristine Angel regains protection from artifacts and from white, blue, red, and green, but not from black for the remainder of that turn.

Protection here means the creature can't be blocked by, targeted by, dealt damage by, enchanted or equipped by anything of that quality. Since Mob is a black instant, and Pristine Angel's protection from black is switched off until end of turn, Mob can legally target Pristine Angel and destroy it (Pristine Angel is a 4/4 with no other protective ability).

Timing caveat: if instead the untap happened on a later turn (i.e., "after combat" meant after that turn ended), Cephalid Snitch's until-end-of-turn effect would have expired, and an untapped Pristine Angel would once again have protection from black — Mob could not target it then. Also note that if Nico casts Mob using convoke and taps creatures, that has no bearing on Pristine Angel's protection.

This analysis rests entirely on the printed card text of Pristine Angel, Cephalid Snitch, and Mob; nothing in the general rules provided contradicts it. Nothing about this changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table.

entries.question: Ashley controls a [Gaea's Liege] and 1 [Bayou]. Naomi controls a [Reverence] and 3 Bayous. Can Ashley attack with the Gaea's Liege?

entries.question: Ares controls [Gaea's Cradle] and no creatures. Nico controls a [Contamination]. If Ares taps the Gaea's Cradle, what mana is produced, if any?

entries.answer:
Ares produces one black mana, {B}.

Why: "To tap a permanent for mana" is defined as activating a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its activation cost — it does not require that the ability actually be capable of producing mana on its own [106.12b]. Gaea's Cradle's ability, "{T}: Add {G} for each creature you control," is still a mana ability even with zero creatures [605.2], and on its own it would produce nothing (zero green mana). Contamination is a replacement effect that reads "If a land is tapped for mana, it produces {B} instead of any other type and amount." Because Ares activated Gaea's Cradle's {T} mana ability, Gaea's Cradle was tapped for mana, and Contamination replaces both the type and the amount — including an amount of zero — so what Gaea's Cradle actually produces is {B}. Contamination's printed text explicitly overrides the amount Gaea's Cradle would otherwise make, so the "{G} for each creature" count is irrelevant.

Note that the mana is added to Ares's mana pool, not Nico's: Contamination only changes what the land produces, not who gets it. Note also that {B} is one black mana specifically, not generic mana, so Ares can spend it only where black or generic costs allow.

Alternate reading, stated plainly: rule 106.12b says the replacement "modifies the mana production event while such an ability is resolving and producing mana," and one could read that as requiring some mana to exist to be replaced, in which case Gaea's Cradle would produce nothing at all under rule 106.5 (an undefined/zero amount yields no mana). I'm going with the reading that Contamination's "instead of any other type and amount" covers an amount of zero, since the card's own text governs.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — Contamination affects any land tapped for mana by any player, so it works the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer one.

entries.answer_gold: No mana is produced. Gaea's Cradle is not producing any mana, so Contamination's replacement effect doesn't apply.

entries.question: Audrey casts [Enlarge] targeting [Goblin Piker], and then attacks with the Goblin Piker. Nico blocks it with a [Baron Sengir], which has gained infect due to their [Grafted Exoskeleton] and indestructible due to their [Withstand Death]. What happens at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Enlarge ends but the -1/-1 counters remain causing Goblin Piker to die, and Baron Sengir’s triggered ability goes on the stack (giving it a +2/+2 counter).
entries.answer:
At end of turn, Goblin Piker dies; Baron Sengir survives and gets a +2/+2 counter.

Setup: Enlarge makes Goblin Piker 9/8 with trample until end of turn. Baron Sengir is 7/7 (5/5 plus Grafted Exoskeleton's +2/+2) with infect and indestructible.

Combat damage: Goblin Piker deals 9 damage to Baron Sengir (assigning lethal to Baron Sengir and any excess trampling over to Nico, if Audrey chooses that assignment). Because Baron Sengir has infect from Grafted Exoskeleton, its 7 damage isn't marked on Goblin Piker — instead Audrey... rather, Nico puts seven -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker (702.90c, 120.4c). Goblin Piker is then 2/1 and survives combat. Baron Sengir has damage marked on it but is indestructible from Withstand Death, so it isn't destroyed.

Cleanup step: all damage marked on permanents is removed and all "until end of turn" effects end simultaneously (514.2, 500.5a). Enlarge's +7/+7 ends, but the seven -1/-1 counters stay — counters aren't a duration effect. Both are applied in layer 7 (613.1g), so Goblin Piker is now 2/1 minus seven = -5/-6. As a state-based action, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner's graveyard, and regeneration can't save it (704.5f) — indestructible wouldn't have helped either, since 0-or-less toughness still kills.

Baron Sengir's triggered ability then triggers, because a creature Baron Sengir dealt damage to this turn died: Nico puts a +2/+2 counter on Baron Sengir. Since a triggered ability triggered during the cleanup step, players get priority and another cleanup step follows. Baron Sengir itself is fine — its marked damage was removed, and it ends the turn as a 9/9 (5/5, +2/+2 from Grafted Exoskeleton, +2/+2 from the counter).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Withstand Death and Grafted Exoskeleton were already applied before combat damage, as stated. If Grafted Exoskeleton had been attached only after combat damage, Baron Sengir's damage would have been ordinary marked damage instead of -1/-1 counters, and Goblin Piker would simply shrink back to 2/1 and survive the turn.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that trample damage goes to the defending player Goblin Piker was attacking.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The effect from Enlarge wears off, but the -1/-1 counters on Goblin Piker remain. Goblin Piker dies. It was dealt damage that turn by Baron Sengir, so Baron Sengir triggers.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Necromancy] that was cast during their declare blockers step. During Aubrey's end step, Nikolai activates [Duskmantle Guildmage]'s first ability. Does Aubrey lose 1 life when the Necromancy is sacrificed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that the delayed triggered ability from Duskmantle Guildmage will cause Aubrey to lose 1 life when Necromancy is sacrificed during the cleanup step (the candidate correctly adds that the creature's subsequent death could cause a second loss).
entries.answer:
Yes — Aubrey loses 1 life when Necromancy is put into their graveyard, and likely a second life if the reanimated creature card is also owned by Aubrey.

Why: Necromancy's own text says that because it was cast when a sorcery couldn't be cast (during the declare blockers step), "the controller of the permanent it becomes sacrifices it at the beginning of the next cleanup step." Sacrificing means Aubrey moves Necromancy from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard [701.21a] [Sacrifice]. That is a card being put into an opponent's graveyard from the standpoint of Nikolai, so Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability — which watches for cards put into an opponent's graveyard from anywhere "this turn" — sees it and Aubrey loses 1 life. The cleanup step is still part of the same turn, and Duskmantle Guildmage's effect is not one that expires at the end of the end step [500.5], so it is still active in cleanup.

Second hit: Necromancy also reads "When this enchantment leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." That leaves-the-battlefield trigger looks back in time and will trigger [603.10a]. When the reanimated creature is sacrificed it goes to its owner's graveyard and dies [Dies] [701.21a]. If that creature card is owned by Aubrey, Duskmantle Guildmage's effect triggers again and Aubrey loses another 1 life; if the creature card is owned by Nikolai or a third player, Duskmantle Guildmage's ability only cares about cards going to an opponent's graveyard, so it triggers for that owner instead (and not at all if that owner is Nikolai himself, since Nikolai is not his own opponent).

Assumed timing: I'm assuming Nikolai activated Duskmantle Guildmage's first ability and let it resolve during Aubrey's end step, before the cleanup step. If it somehow never resolved before the sacrifice, the delayed watcher wouldn't be in place and no life would be lost.

Multiplayer note: the provided rules are not two-player-specific here; Duskmantle Guildmage's ability applies to any of Nikolai's opponents, so at a bigger table the life loss follows whoever owns each card going to a graveyard, as long as that owner is an opponent of Nikolai.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Duskmantle Guildmage creates a delayed triggered ability. The existence of that ability is not a continuous effect, so it still exists during the cleanup step.

entries.question: Alma casts [Virulent Wound], targeting Nico's [Bronze Sable]. In response, Nico casts [Brute Strength] on the Bronze Sable. What happens at the end of the turn?
